title: How a pawn captures
introduction: A pawn captures one square diagonally forward. The white pawn on e4 can capture the black pawn on d5.

moves.explanation: The pawn moves diagonally to d5 and removes the black pawn.

title: The knight's move
introduction: A knight moves in an L shape: two squares in one direction and one square sideways. It can jump over other pieces.

moves.explanation: The knight moves from b2 to c4: two ranks forward and one file sideways.

title: How a rook captures
introduction: The rook on d2 can move along the clear d-file and capture the rook on d5.

moves.explanation: The white rook stops on d5 and removes the black rook. A rook cannot jump over a piece.

title: How a bishop captures
introduction: The bishop on c1 can reach the knight on f4 along a clear diagonal.

moves.explanation: Bxf4 captures the knight. The bishop stayed on the same colour of square throughout its move.

title: Promoting a pawn
introduction: When a pawn reaches the far rank, its player chooses a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Here White chooses a queen.

moves.explanation: The pawn reaches a8 and becomes a queen. The new queen gives check along the eighth rank.

title: Castling kingside
introduction: Castling moves the king toward a rook and brings that rook into play. The king and rook must retain castling rights.

moves.explanation: White castles: the king moves to g1 and the rook moves to f1. The king may not castle out of, through, or into check.

title: Castling queenside
introduction: Black can castle toward the a-file rook if the squares between them are empty and the king's route is safe.

moves.explanation: Black castles queenside: the king moves to c8 and the rook to d8.

title: En passant
introduction: Black has just moved the pawn from d7 to d5. White may capture it as if it had advanced one square.

moves.explanation: The e5 pawn lands on d6 while the black pawn on d5 is removed. En passant must be played immediately or the chance is lost.

title: A rook promotion avoids stalemate
introduction: White is winning, but c8=Q would immediately stalemate Black. A rook is enough to keep the win.

moves.explanation: c8=R avoids stalemate. With a queen on c8, Black would have no legal move and the king would not be in check.
Ka6 is Black’s only legal move.
Ra8# is checkmate: the rook checks on the a-file and the white king controls b5, b6 and b7.

title: Capture and promote
introduction: A pawn can capture diagonally onto the final rank and promote on that same move.

moves.explanation: axb8=Q captures the rook and promotes to a queen. The new queen checks the king along the eighth rank.

title: Escaping check
introduction: The rook checks along the e-file. White can escape by moving the king to an unattacked square.

moves.explanation: Kf2 leaves the rook’s line. A king cannot move to a square controlled by an enemy piece.
Black places the rook on e5. White has escaped the check and still has an active rook.
Rd8+ illustrates how White can give a check of their own.

title: Blocking a check
introduction: A sliding piece’s check can be stopped by a protected piece placed between the attacker and the king.

moves.explanation: Be3 blocks the e-file. The knight on c4 protects the bishop on e3.
If Black plays Rxe3+, the rook captures the bishop but lands on a square defended by the knight.
Nxe3 captures the rook. Blocking with a defended piece prevents Black from winning the bishop for free.

title: Capturing the checker
introduction: The rook on e2 checks the white king. Here no black piece protects the rook.

moves.explanation: Kxe2 removes the attacker. A king may make this capture only when the destination square is not attacked.

title: A simple checkmate
introduction: White's queen and king work together to restrict the black king's escape squares.

moves.explanation: Qg7# is checkmate: the king is in check, cannot capture the protected queen, and has no safe square.

title: Back-rank checkmate
introduction: Black's own pawns restrict the king. White's rook can exploit the weak back rank.

moves.explanation: Rd8# checks along the eighth rank. Black's pawns occupy the king's flight squares and cannot stop the check.

title: Stalemate is a draw
introduction: White is winning, but the next queen move accidentally draws. No legal move is checkmate only when the king is also in check.

moves.explanation: Black has no legal move, but the king is not in check: this is stalemate, and the game is a draw.

title: A knight fork
introduction: A fork attacks two pieces at once. The knight can attack the black king and queen together.

moves.explanation: Ne6+ checks the king on g7 and attacks the queen on c7.
Black must answer the check; in this example the king moves to h6.
Nxc7 captures the queen that the knight attacked.

title: An absolute pin
introduction: A pinned piece cannot move if that would expose its own king to check.

moves.explanation: Bb5 aligns the bishop, knight and king on one diagonal. The knight on c6 is absolutely pinned.
Kf7 moves the king off the diagonal, ending the absolute pin.
Bxc6 captures the knight. The example illustrates the alignment; it does not claim this defence is forced.

title: A rook skewer
introduction: In a skewer, an attack on a valuable front piece exposes another target behind it. The bishop on c6 guards a8.

moves.explanation: Ra1+ checks the king on a7 with the queen behind it on a8.
The king leaves the a-file. Kb8 is also legal, but the bishop protects a8 against the king.
Rxa8 captures the exposed queen; the bishop protects the rook, and the pawn on b5 protects the bishop.

title: Discovered double check
introduction: The bishop blocks its own rook's line to the black king. Moving it can reveal the rook's attack.

moves.explanation: Bb5+ also opens the e-file. Both bishop and rook check the king at the same time.
In a double check the king must move; blocking or capturing just one checker is not enough.

title: Develop pieces and control the centre
introduction: In the opening, develop pieces, contest central squares and prepare to castle. This is one possible sequence.

moves.explanation: e4 claims central space and opens lines for the bishop and queen.
Black contests the centre with e5.
Nf3 develops a knight and attacks the e5 pawn.
Nc6 develops and defends the pawn.
Bc4 develops the bishop toward the centre and helps White prepare kingside castling.

title: Finish development safely
introduction: Both sides have developed a knight and bishop. White can now castle kingside.

moves.explanation: O-O moves the king to safety and brings the rook to f1.
Black develops the knight and attacks the e4 pawn.
Re1 places the rook on the central e-file. This is one illustrative continuation.

title: The f7 weakness
introduction: The f7 pawn is defended only by Black's king at the start. This familiar sequence shows why both sides must watch it.

moves.explanation: e4 opens the bishop's diagonal.
Black also takes space in the centre.
Qh5 points at e5 and f7, but early queen moves can be chased by developing pieces.
Nc6 develops a knight and protects e5.
Bc4 adds pressure against f7.
Nf6 attacks the queen but misses the immediate threat.
Qxf7# is mate: the bishop protects the queen. Black can avoid this by defending f7 earlier.

title: King opposition
introduction: The kings face each other with one square between them. Black must move first and give way; this is called opposition.

moves.explanation: Black's king steps aside, allowing White to advance.
White follows while keeping distance between the kings. Opposition is often useful in king-and-pawn endings.

title: Advancing a passed pawn
introduction: A passed pawn has no opposing pawns ahead of it on its file or either adjacent file.

moves.explanation: White advances the passed pawn.
The black king moves toward the pawn's path.
The pawn reaches the seventh rank; the white king helps control nearby squares.
The king steps away from the promotion square.
The pawn reaches the eighth rank and promotes to a queen.
